dcf.method: 5-year FCFF: EBITDA - tax on EBIT - capex - change in net working capital; growth fades linearly from the starting rate to the year-5 rate; Gordon terminal value; equity = EV - borrowings.

reverse_dcf.note: Constant sales growth for five years, at the base margin and the same WACC and terminal growth, that makes the DCF equal today's EV.

blocks.text: [F] Apsis Aerocom is a Bengaluru build-to-print precision machining shop. It machines components and does small assemblies on 3-, 4- and 5-axis CNC centres to customer drawings for aerospace, defence and healthcare-equipment customers (AR2026 p.5, p.6). [F] Every product is made to the customer's specification against confirmed orders and sold direct, with no distributors (AR2026 p.5). [F] The company makes money by converting bar and billet into finished parts. In FY26 product sales were Rs 30.04 cr and services Rs 0.61 cr of Rs 30.65 cr revenue (AR2026 p.89). [MC] Management says the customer owns the CAD design and Apsis owns the CAM machining process, which is where it claims its stickiness comes from (CALL Jun 2026).

blocks.text: Source: segment values (PPT Jun 2026); percentages are our calculation. [F] Geographically the business is almost entirely domestic. FOB exports were Rs 2.56 lakh in FY26, against Rs 20.66 lakh in FY25 (AR2026 p.34, p.93), or about 0.1% of revenue [E]. [MC] The MD says most orders come from foreign OEMs working through Indian joint ventures under defence offsets, and that 90% of components are delivered within India for the Air Force, Navy and other defence uses (CALL Jun 2026). [F] The customer base is small and concentrated. The top customer was 35.59% of FY26 revenue, the top 5 were 87.37% and the top 10 were 96.97% (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.102). [MC] Management puts the customer count at 15 to 20 (CALL Jun 2026).

Listing status: [F] Apsis listed on the NSE Emerge SME platform on 18 March 2026 through a Rs 35.77 cr fresh issue at Rs 110 per share (AR2026 p.24-25). [F] As an SME-listed company it reports half-yearly, is exempt from Regulations 17-27 corporate-governance reporting and publishes no BRSR (AR2026 p.35, p.37). [AI] The evidence base is therefore thin: four years of company financials, three half-year data points, one earnings call and one annual report. The offer document (DRHP/RHP) was not available to us.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. Valuation already discounts the aspiration. [F] At Rs 612 the stock trades at 98.1x trailing earnings and 24.2x EV/sales (NUMBERS). [E] The reverse DCF needs about 77% annual sales growth for five years, against 19.8% in the base case (NUMBERS). [E] That is roughly the 75% CAGR implied by management's Rs 500 cr FY31 aspiration (CALL Jun 2026). Even the bull DCF value of Rs 153.2 is 75% below the price (NUMBERS).

2. Customer concentration has shifted, not fallen. [F] The top two customers were 69.62% of FY26 revenue against 74.38% in FY25. The second-largest customer rose from 22.35% to 34.03% (AR2026 p.102). [E] The top customer's revenue was flat at about Rs 10.9 cr, while customer #2 grew from about Rs 4.6 cr to about Rs 10.4 cr.

3. The pre-IPO year's profits were not cash. [F] FY25 CFO was Rs 0.05 cr against PAT of Rs 6.60 cr (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.74). [F] FY25 EBITDA margin of 49.8% included a Rs 1.61 cr credit from WIP/finished-goods build-up (AR2026 p.72, p.90). [E] That credit was about 16% of FY25 EBITDA.

4. Management's reason for the margin drop does not match the P&L. [MC] The CFO blamed Unit II fixed costs, listing costs and raw materials (CALL Jun 2026). [E] About 11 of the 12.3-point EBITDA-margin decline came from the material and job-work ratio: a smaller inventory-build credit plus higher consumption. Other expenses stayed at 10.8% of revenue (AR2026 p.72, p.91).

5. Old trade payables and a balance-confirmation key audit matter. [F] Rs 2.05 cr of Rs 3.14 cr non-MSME payables are overdue by more than two years (AR2026 p.85). [F] The auditor made receivable and payable balances, including deemed confirmations, a key audit matter (AR2026 p.56). [F] The notes say balances are subject to confirmation (AR2026 p.101).

6. Company documents disagree on core facts. [F] Unit II capex is Rs 27.02 cr in the IPO objects (AR2026 p.25; PPT Jun 2026) but 'approximately 60 crore' on the call (CALL Jun 2026). [F] Unit I capacity is 1,50,000 components (AR2026 p.12) against 1,20,000 (PPT Jun 2026). [F] Unit II adds about 3,00,000 (AR2026 p.12) against about 1,80,000 (PPT Jun 2026). [F] The annual report says Unit II was commissioned (AR2026 p.15), but the call says operations start in Q2 FY27 (CALL Jun 2026).

7. Unit II sits on a short lease. [F] The Unit II building is on leasehold KIADB land whose lease runs only to June 2030. The building is depreciated over 30 years on the assumption of renewal (AR2026 p.62, p.87).

8. The finance function and board are thin. [F] The CFO is 28 with about two years' experience in accounts and finance (AR2026 p.20, p.39). [F] Internal audit covered only Q4 FY26 (AR2026 p.65). [F] The POSH internal committee had not been constituted (AR2026 p.26).

9. Directors' pay is rising fast. [F] Director remuneration rose from Rs 0.68 cr to Rs 1.35 cr (AR2026 p.90). [F] Managerial pay rose 64% while non-managerial median pay rose 2.71% (AR2026 p.39). [E] Director pay equals about 18% of FY26 PAT.

10. Liquidity and float. [F] The company has 307 shareholders and 18.72% public holding (NUMBERS). [F] The stock sits near its 52-week high of Rs 625, against a low of Rs 147 (NUMBERS). [AI] Exit liquidity for institutional-size positions is doubtful.

Is Unit II a doubling of revenue or a doubling of fixed cost? [MC] Management targets Rs 48 cr in FY27 and about Rs 60 cr incremental revenue in FY28 (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] The market may be under-weighting ramp risk: machine lead times are 6-10 months, the machine count is stated three different ways, and the order book covers only one year. It may equally be under-weighting how quickly a constrained shop fills new capacity if the orders are real.

Is 37-40% EBITDA sustainable? [MC] Management says yes (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] The FY25 margin was flattered by inventory build, and the H1 FY26 margin was 35.0% (NUMBERS). A fair debate is whether the steady state is mid-30s rather than 40%.

Is concentration falling? [MC] Management says the top customer fell from 52% to 35% (CALL Jun 2026). [E] Two customers still account for about 70% (AR2026 p.102). The bull reading is that a second anchor has become large. The bear reading is dependence on two programmes.

Is this defence, or build-to-print job work? [F] The company holds no NADCAP and does no special processes (CALL Jun 2026), and customers own the design (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] Value capture is in machining know-how, not IP. That argues for a machining-shop multiple, not a defence-platform multiple.

Is the 500 cr aspiration informative? [MC] Management is 'very, very much confident' of Rs 500 cr by FY31 (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] No capacity, capex or order evidence in the documents supports it. Unit I, II and III together are framed at about 30 + 60 + 70 cr (CALL Jun 2026).

blocks.text: [AI] The consensus narrative, visible in the 91x IPO subscription (AR2026 p.9) and a share price about 5.6x the Rs 110 issue price (NUMBERS), treats Apsis as a defence-indigenisation compounder. Our reading is narrower. It is a well-run, capacity-constrained build-to-print machining shop of about Rs 31 cr revenue with two dominant customers. Its reported pre-IPO profitability was flattered by inventory build and not converted to cash, and its disclosures contain unreconciled inconsistencies. [E] The shares price in close to full delivery of management's Rs 500 cr FY31 aspiration, which the documents do not substantiate beyond Unit II. The underlying business may well be good. The mismatch is between what is evidenced (Rs 48 cr FY27 target, Rs 40.5 cr order book) and what is priced (NUMBERS reverse DCF).

subsections.title: Where value is captured and why

blocks.text: [AI] Value is captured at process qualification. Once a component's machining route is approved by an OEM, re-sourcing requires new first-article inspection and audits, which creates switching friction. That fits management's claim of sole-supplier status on about 40% of revenue (CALL Jun 2026). [E] FY26 EBITDA margin of 37.5% (NUMBERS) is high for job-shop machining. [F] The company has no design IP (CALL Jun 2026) and does not register material IP (AR2026 p.24). The margin therefore rests on know-how and qualification rather than ownership.

[F] Purchases include job-work expenses. Purchases and job work were Rs 11.33 cr in FY26 against Rs 6.24 cr in FY25 (AR2026 p.90); the split is not disclosed. [F] Fixed-asset turnover was 2.49x in FY26, and capex was 20.1% of sales (NUMBERS). [F] Unit II is funded with Rs 27.02 cr of IPO proceeds for machinery (AR2026 p.25). [AI] This is capital-intensive relative to revenue. Each rupee of machinery supports roughly two to three rupees of annual revenue, so growth requires continuous capex.

[MC] The MD says the majority of revenue is complex parts, but the company also accepts non-complex and medium-complex parts to satisfy existing customers (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] Any part that can be made on commercially available 3-axis machines to a customer drawing is commodity-like. The differentiated share is the 5-axis, tight-tolerance, sole-source work, which management sizes at about 40% of revenue (CALL Jun 2026) but does not document. The absence of special processes means Apsis does not capture the harder-to-replicate stages.

subsections.title: Currency, trade policy and location risk

blocks.text: [F] Foreign-exchange outgo was Rs 5.45 cr in FY26: raw materials Rs 1.14 cr and capital goods Rs 4.32 cr (AR2026 p.93). [MC] Unit II machines mostly come from Europe and Japan with 6-10 month lead times (CALL Jun 2026). [MC] The CFO cited raw-material inflation from geopolitical disruption and forex fluctuations, 'particularly in the US and European markets' (CALL Jun 2026). [AI] The company is short foreign currency on inputs and capex with no natural export hedge. No hedging policy is disclosed. [F] The EPCG export obligation of Rs 2.34 cr must be met within six years of availing the benefit; the contingent duty is Rs 16.14 lakh (AR2026 p.93). [E] At FY26 export levels the obligation would not be met. [F] Tariff or trade-policy events are not discussed in the documents. [AI] Both plants are in Bengaluru, about 40 km apart, so there is regional concentration risk (power, labour, KIADB policy).
Sources: (PPT Jun 2026; AR2026 p.102). [F] FY23-FY24 concentration is not disclosed in the documents available.

That makes revenue sensitive to offset-policy timing and to individual programme schedules rather than to the aggregate defence budget. What exists today is qualified supply of machined parts on a handful of programmes. The larger 'defence manufacturing under Atmanirbhar Bharat' positioning is narrative (CALL Jun 2026).
